title: Reaction time
aim: To plan and carry out an investigation into the effect of a factor (drinking a caffeinated drink) on human reaction time, using the ruler drop test.
background: Reaction time is the time between a stimulus and a response. In the ruler drop test the stimulus is seeing the ruler start to fall. The light is detected by receptors in the retina of the eye, and impulses travel along a sensory neurone to the brain (part of the central nervous system). The brain coordinates a response and sends impulses along a motor neurone to the effectors, the muscles in the hand, which contract to catch the ruler.

Catching the ruler is a conscious, voluntary response, not a reflex, because it involves the brain making a decision. Reflexes are automatic and rapid, and do not involve the conscious part of the brain. A typical reaction time for catching a ruler is about 0.15 to 0.25 seconds.

The distance the ruler falls before it is caught is used to find reaction time: the further it falls, the longer the reaction time. The distance is converted to a time using a conversion table (calculated from the equation of motion for a falling object). Factors such as caffeine, tiredness, practice, distractions or using the non-dominant hand can affect reaction time. Caffeine is a stimulant and is expected to shorten reaction time.
hypothesis: Drinking a caffeinated drink will decrease reaction time, so the ruler will fall a shorter distance before it is caught after the drink than before it.

variables.independent: Whether the person has drunk a caffeinated drink (reaction time measured before, and 10 minutes after, drinking a caffeinated drink).
variables.dependent: Reaction time (s), found from the distance the ruler falls before being caught (cm) using a conversion table.
control: Same person catching the ruler, using the same (dominant) hand
Same ruler, dropped from the same starting position (0 cm level with the top of the catcher's thumb)
Same gap between thumb and finger (about 2 cm) and forearm resting on the edge of the table
Same person dropping the ruler, with no warning and a varied delay before release
Same environment with no distractions, and the same volume of drink
Same time interval between drinking and testing (10 minutes)

equipment: 30 cm ruler (or metre ruler) with 0 cm at one end
Caffeinated drink (for example a can of cola or a cup of coffee) and a measuring cylinder to measure the volume
Stopwatch or clock to time the 10 minute wait
Conversion table of distance fallen against reaction time
method: Check that the person being tested (the catcher) is happy to take part, does not have a medical condition that makes caffeine unsuitable, and has not had any caffeine for several hours. Carry out the test in a classroom, not a laboratory, because a drink is involved.
The catcher sits on a chair with their dominant forearm resting on the table, so that their hand sticks out over the edge.
The catcher holds their thumb and first finger about 2 cm apart.
The tester holds a ruler vertically at the top end, so that the 0 cm mark is level with the top of the catcher's thumb and the ruler hangs between the thumb and finger without touching them.
The catcher looks at the ruler, not at the tester's hand. The tester drops the ruler without warning, waiting a different length of time before each drop so the catcher cannot predict it.
The catcher catches the ruler as quickly as possible between thumb and finger.
Read the distance on the ruler at the top of the catcher's thumb, to the nearest 0.5 cm, and record it.
Repeat the test four more times (five drops in total) and calculate the mean distance.
The catcher then drinks a measured volume of the caffeinated drink and waits 10 minutes.
Repeat the ruler drop five more times, in exactly the same way, and record the distances.
Use the conversion table to convert each distance into a reaction time, and calculate the mean reaction time before and after the caffeinated drink.
Ideally, repeat with several different people (or compare with a group who drink a decaffeinated drink) to see whether the pattern is the same.

safety.risk: Can cause a raised heart rate, anxiety or sleep problems, and may be harmful to people with some medical conditions.
safety.precaution: Use only a normal serving of the drink, check with the participant and teacher beforehand, and do not include anyone who should avoid caffeine or who does not want to take part.

safety.hazard: Eating or drinking where chemicals have been used
safety.risk: Swallowing harmful substances from a contaminated laboratory bench or container.
safety.precaution: Carry out the drinking part in a classroom, not a laboratory, using clean cups that have never been used for chemicals.

safety.risk: A metre ruler could hit someone's foot or eye.
safety.precaution: Use a 30 cm ruler where possible, keep feet clear, and do not drop the ruler near faces.

results.notes: Conversion table (distance fallen → reaction time): 5 cm → 0.101 s; 10 cm → 0.143 s; 15 cm → 0.175 s; 20 cm → 0.202 s; 25 cm → 0.226 s; 30 cm → 0.247 s. The table is calculated using t = √(2d ÷ g), with d in metres and g = 9.8 m/s². Because the relationship is not linear, convert each distance to a time and then calculate the mean time. Display the results as a bar chart of mean reaction time before and after the drink.

analysis: The mean distance fallen decreased from 19 cm before the caffeinated drink to 14 cm after it, so the mean reaction time decreased from 0.197 s to 0.169 s. This supports the hypothesis that caffeine decreases reaction time.
Caffeine is a stimulant that increases activity in the nervous system, so impulses are passed along the pathway from receptor to effector more quickly, and the response is faster.

The decrease in mean reaction time is 0.028 s, which is about a 14% decrease. The ranges of the two sets of results do not overlap (0.186 to 0.207 s before and 0.156 to 0.181 s after), so the difference is likely to be real rather than due to random variation.

However, the second set of results might also be faster because the catcher had practised. To be confident that caffeine caused the change, a control group should drink a decaffeinated drink and be tested in the same way, and the investigation should be repeated with many people.

The pathway for this response is: stimulus (falling ruler) → receptors (light-sensitive cells in the retina) → sensory neurone → brain (coordinator) → motor neurone → effector (hand muscles) → response (catching the ruler).

errors.error: The catcher may anticipate the drop, for example by watching the tester's hand, giving an unrealistically short reaction time.
errors.improvement: Vary the time before each drop, tell the catcher to look only at the ruler, and do not give any warning.

errors.error: Improvement after the drink could be caused by practice (learning) rather than by caffeine.
errors.improvement: Give several practice drops before recording results, and use a control group who drink a decaffeinated drink.

errors.error: The starting position of the ruler or the gap between thumb and finger may vary between drops.
errors.improvement: Line the 0 cm mark up with the top of the thumb every time, and keep the forearm resting on the table edge.

errors.error: Results from one person may not be representative because reaction times vary between people and with tiredness or caffeine tolerance.
errors.improvement: Test a larger sample of people of similar age, at the same time of day, who have not had caffeine beforehand.

errors.error: Reading the distance by eye can be imprecise, especially if the ruler is caught at an angle.
errors.improvement: Read the scale at the top of the thumb at eye level, or use a computer-based reaction timer for greater precision.

examTips: Catching a ruler is not a reflex: it is a conscious response coordinated by the brain. Reflexes are automatic and do not involve the conscious part of the brain.
A greater distance fallen means a longer (slower) reaction time. Use the conversion table to change each distance into a time.
Learn the pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → coordinator (brain) → motor neurone → effector → response.
When evaluating, mention the practice effect, anticipation of the drop and differences between people, and suggest a control group (such as a decaffeinated drink).
Reaction times are often quoted in milliseconds: multiply seconds by 1000 (0.2 s = 200 ms).

questions.question: Why should the tester drop the ruler without any warning?
options: So the catcher cannot predict when it will fall and reacts only to seeing it move
So the catcher uses their dominant hand
So the ruler does not touch the catcher's fingers
markScheme: 1 mark: so the catcher cannot anticipate the drop (and responds only to the stimulus of the ruler moving)
questions.explanation: If the catcher can predict the drop, they may start closing their fingers before the ruler moves, giving a falsely short reaction time. The ruler falls at the same rate however it is released.

questions.question:
A student measured their reaction time five times using the ruler drop test.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean distance fallen by the ruler.
questions.explanation: Add the five distances (100 cm) and divide by 5, giving a mean of 20 cm.

questions.question:
In a ruler drop test the ruler fell 20 cm before it was caught.
Calculate the reaction time.
Use the equation:
t = √(2d ÷ g)
where d is the distance fallen in metres and g = 9.8 m/s²
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Convert cm to m first (0.20 m). Then 2 × 0.20 ÷ 9.8 = 0.0408, and the square root is 0.202 s, which is 0.20 s to 2 significant figures. Using 20 instead of 0.20 gives an impossible answer of about 2 s.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the pathway when a student catches the falling ruler?
options: Receptor → motor neurone → brain → sensory neurone → effector
Effector → sensory neurone → brain → motor neurone → receptor
Receptor → sensory neurone → brain → motor neurone → effector
Brain → receptor → sensory neurone → effector → motor neurone
markScheme: 1 mark: receptor → sensory neurone → brain (CNS) → motor neurone → effector
questions.explanation: Receptors in the eye detect the stimulus, the sensory neurone carries impulses to the brain, the brain coordinates a response, and the motor neurone carries impulses to the effector (hand muscles).

questions.question: Name the effector in the ruler drop test.
markScheme: 1 mark: muscles (in the hand / fingers / arm)
questions.explanation: Effectors are muscles or glands that bring about a response. Here the muscles of the hand contract to close the thumb and finger on the ruler. The hand itself is not the effector: its muscles are.

questions.question: Why is catching a falling ruler NOT a reflex action?
options: It involves the conscious part of the brain deciding to respond
It does not involve any neurones
It involves a gland as the effector
It is much faster than a reflex
markScheme: 1 mark: it is a conscious (voluntary) action involving the brain
questions.explanation: Reflexes are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain. Catching the ruler is a voluntary decision, which is why it is slower than a reflex such as pulling a hand away from a hot object.

Figure 1 shows how the ruler drop test is set up.
Give two variables that should be kept the same when measuring the reaction time of one person.

markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: same hand; same ruler; same starting position (0 cm at top of thumb); same gap between thumb and finger; same person dropping; forearm resting on table edge; no distractions; same time after the drink
questions.explanation: Each of these could change the distance the ruler falls, so they must be controlled for the investigation to be a fair test of the effect of caffeine.

questions.question:
A student measured their reaction time before and after a caffeinated drink.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage decrease in reaction time.
questions.explanation: Percentage change = change ÷ original value × 100. Divide by the original value (0.200 s), not the new value; dividing by 0.170 gives 17.6%, which is wrong.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a student's reaction times in five ruler drop tests.
Explain why the ruler drop test is repeated five times and a mean is calculated.
markScheme: 1 mark: reaction time varies from one attempt to the next (random variation)
1 mark: a mean reduces the effect of random errors / allows anomalies to be spotted, giving a more accurate (representative) value
questions.explanation: One catch could be unusually fast (a lucky guess) or slow (a distraction). Repeating and averaging makes the result closer to the person's true reaction time.

questions.question:
A student's reaction time was 0.25 s.
Give this reaction time in milliseconds (ms).
questions.explanation: There are 1000 milliseconds in one second, so multiply by 1000: 0.25 × 1000 = 250 ms.

questions.question:
A student's reaction time was shorter after drinking cola.
Suggest why this does not prove that caffeine caused the shorter reaction time.
markScheme: 1 mark: the student may have improved through practice (or the cola contains sugar, which could also have an effect)
1 mark: there was no control, such as a group drinking decaffeinated cola, or only one person was tested
questions.explanation: Other variables changed at the same time as the caffeine. A control group drinking a decaffeinated version of the same drink would show whether caffeine itself caused the improvement.

questions.question:
Two students did the ruler drop test.
Table 1 shows the results.
What do the results show?
options: Student A has a longer reaction time than Student B
Student B reacted twice as quickly as Student A
Both students have the same reaction time
Student A has a shorter reaction time than Student B
markScheme: 1 mark: Student A has a shorter reaction time
questions.explanation: The ruler falls further the longer it takes to catch it, so a shorter distance means a shorter (faster) reaction time. The time is not simply proportional to the distance (it depends on its square root), so 24 cm is not twice the time of 12 cm.

questions.question: Describe the role of the brain in catching the ruler.
markScheme: 1 mark: the brain (central nervous system) is the coordinator: it receives impulses from the sensory neurone
1 mark: it sends impulses along a motor neurone to the effector (hand muscles)
questions.explanation: The brain processes the information from the eye and coordinates a response, sending impulses to the muscles to contract.

questions.question: Plan an investigation to find out whether drinking a caffeinated drink affects a person's reaction time, using a ruler.
markScheme: Indicative content: catcher sits with forearm on table edge, hand over edge; thumb and finger a set distance apart; tester holds ruler vertically with 0 cm at top of thumb; drop without warning; record distance at top of thumb; repeat several times and calculate mean; convert distance to reaction time using conversion table; drink a measured volume of caffeinated drink; wait a set time (for example 10 minutes); repeat the test in the same way; compare mean reaction times before and after; control variables: same hand, same ruler, same starting position, same tester, no distractions; control group with decaffeinated drink or practice drops first; test several people; safety: check caffeine is suitable, drink in classroom not laboratory

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered plan that would give valid results, including the ruler drop technique, repeats and means, conversion to reaction time, measurements before and after the drink, and control variables.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a plan with most key steps, but missing detail such as control variables, repeats or conversion to time.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as dropping a ruler before and after a drink, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The highest marks need both a clear ruler drop technique and a valid comparison: before and after (or caffeinated and decaffeinated), with repeats, controls and conversion of distances to times.

questions.question:
A class of 30 students measured their reaction times using their dominant hand.
They then repeated the test using their non-dominant hand.
Figure 1 shows the results.
Evaluate whether these results show that people react faster with their dominant hand.

markScheme: Indicative content: supporting: mean reaction time shorter for dominant hand by 0.03 s; large sample of 30 students makes the means more reliable; same test method used. Against: dominant hand always tested first, so practice effect would make the non-dominant hand faster, not slower, which strengthens the conclusion, but tiredness or boredom could make the second test slower; difference is small, need to know the spread or range of results to see if the difference is significant; students are all of similar age so may not apply to all people; different testers may drop differently; to improve, test hands in a random or alternating order
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a balanced evaluation using the data, considering at least one strength and one limitation, and reaching a justified conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement that the dominant hand was faster, or a single limitation, with little use of data.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Evaluate means weighing up evidence. The sample size supports the conclusion, but the order of testing and the small difference without information about spread are weaknesses. Testing hands in a random order would remove the order effect.
